items.title: Muru
items.content: Muru Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production. As he did with wrapture , he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process. Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks: 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read: The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too. items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.content: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.content: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . Via Lobste.rs Tags: mysql , postgresql , replication , scaling , wikipedia , ai-security-research

items.title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
items.content: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.content: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. items.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
items.content: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists , because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file . The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it ( %23 is a URL-encoded # ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README . I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty. Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022 , originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML . This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers . These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset

items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.content: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

items.title: datasette 1.0a43
items.content: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) items.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
items.content: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models: In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
items.content: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. items.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
items.content: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.content: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.content: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.content: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.content: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . items.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.content: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox , html , mozilla , datasette

items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.content: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. items.title: llm 0.37
items.content: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721 , ac1982 , Allen Flux , Bian Yuhan , Bishop Kammeraad , Chen Yufeiyang , Christopher Krah , Ethan Stoner , Jiachen Xie , Olamide Faniyan , Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu , nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release! items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.content: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. Tags: census , surveys , ai , generative-ai , llms

items.title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
items.content: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. items.title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
items.content: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. Via Hacker News Tags: iframes , javascript , sandboxing , security , xss , openai , chatgpt , content-security-policy

items.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.content: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.content: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

items.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
items.content: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. items.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
items.content: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it. It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here's that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here's that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here's that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave". Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here

items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
items.content: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. Here are the pelicans for the different reasoning levels. This pelican for "max" cost 11.3161 cents and took 4 minutes and 11 seconds: Here's a new comparison grid showing pelicans for every reasoning level of OpenAI's current frontier lineup: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna. GPT-6.1 Terra is priced at $1/million input tokens and $5/million output - almost half the price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and around 10x the price of GPT-6 Luna. items.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
items.content: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers , go , javascript , jeff-lindsay , shot-scraper

items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.content: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). items.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
items.content: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal. August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress. August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team. September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix. October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available. October 21, 2026: Public disclosure. Via Hacker News Tags: open-source , php , security , ai , ai-security-research

items.title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
items.content: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum.
